utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] The hearing is open. Madam Registrar, please introduce the case for this hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This case concerns the Prosecutor against Dragan Nikolic No. IT-94-2-R61.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] This concerns Rule 61 of the Rules of procedure, so I now turn to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I appear as Prosecutor with Mr. Niemann and Miss McHenry. Your Honours, as you have just mentioned, this is the first proceeding under Rule 61 before this Tribunal. Such a proceeding, a Rule 61 proceeding, has been designed by your Honours and your colleagues to cater for the situation where a warrant of arrest issued by the Tribunal against an indicted accused has not been executed. The need for such a procedure arises because the Security Council on the advice of the Secretary-General, wisely set its face against trials in absentia. In his report to the Council in May 1993, the Secretary-General stated in paragraph 101, I quote: "A trial should not commence until the accused is physically present before the International Tribunal. This is a widespread perception that trials in absentia should not be provided for in the statute as this would not be consistent with Article 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which provides that the accused shall be entitled to be tried in his presence". Your Honours, I would submit that other convincing reasons could also have been found to justify the decisio not to make provision for trials in absentia. Such trials tend not to satisfy calls for justice and create an impression of being "show trials". The evidence is untested and any conviction and sentence that may follow are empty shells and would be so perceived. If the person "convicted" is later arrested and brought for trial the earlier proceedings would have to be disregarded and a trial would begin de novo. An international tribunal has no police force and no means itself to enforce warrants of arrests issued by it. It must necessarily rely for that purpose upon the co-operation of Member States of the United Nations; notwithstanding the peremptory obligations of States to comply with Chapter VII resolutions of the Security Council, the possibility was foreseen that a Member State might refuse or fail so to comply or the political and military situation might be such that a willing Member State may be physically incapable of making its co-operation effective. The question which, therefore, required consideration by the Judges was whether in the event of the non-execution of a warrant, the Tribunal should allow its process to remain indefinitely suspended or whether there was some action, short of a trial in absentia, that could be taken by it. In that context the Judges fashioned the innovative provisions of Rule 61. Rule 61 provides that a Judge of a Trial Chamber shall order the indictment to be submitted to that Chamber if the Prosecutor has taken all reasonable steps to effect personal service of the indictment, including recourse t the appropriate authorities of the State in whose territory or under whose jurisdiction and control the person resides or was last known to be, and the Prosecutor has otherwise tried to inform the accused of the existence of the indictment by seeking publication of newspaper advertisements pursuant to Rule 60. Upon obtaining that order the Prosecutor is obliged to submit the indictment to the Trial Chamber in open court, together with all the evidence that was before the Judge who initially confirmed the indictment. Additional evidence may also be placed before the Trial Chamber, including the viva voce evidence of witnesses. If, on that evidence, the Trial Chamber is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused has committed all or any of the crimes charged in the indictment, it shall so determine. The relevant parts of the indictment are required to be read out by the Prosecutor together with an account of the efforts to effect service of the warrant of arrest. If the Trial Chamber is so satisfied, in other words, that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused has committed all or any of the crimes charged in the indictment, the Trial Chamber shall issue an international warrant in respect of the accused which shall be transmitted to all States. In addition, if the Prosecutor satisfies the Trial Chamber that the failure to execute the warrant was due in whole or in part to a failure or refusal of a State to co-operate with the Tribunal, the Trial Chamber shall so certify, in which event the President of the Tribuna shall notify the Security Council. Your Honours, as one would expect, the Rules of the Tribunal do not attempt to prescribe appropriate action by the Security Council in the event of a notification to it by the President under Rule 61. The Charter, however, gives a wide discretion to the Security Council in such an event and obviously the imposition of sanctions or at least the threat of sanctions is the kind of action that readily comes to mind. The effect of Rule 61 is to ensure that an accused who decides not to appear for trial cannot thereby prevent the Tribunal from making public the evidence upon which he or she has been indicted. It also enables the Tribunal to take effective steps to ensure that neither an accused nor a Member State may, with impunity, ignore a warrant issued by the Tribunal. I referred earlier to the provisions of Rule 61 being innovative. They are also historic in that they cater for a situation which has never ever before arisen. The Nuremberg and Tokyo Trials are only comparable proceedings in which it was sought to enforce international humanitarian law. Those were military tribunals and the victorious powers were able themselves to execute warrants of arrest and detain those accused of war crimes. This Tribunal is a civil and not a military organ and it is not acting on behalf of any one or a combination of States. Through the Security Council it is truly acting on behalf of the whole international communities. It is for those reasons that the Judges of this Tribunal were faced with the uniquely new situation whic called for an innovative approach. While in no way constituting a trial in absentia, Rule 61 proceedings have other important consequences. A warrant of arrest issued by the Tribunal in consequence of the confirmation of an indictment is directed to the State where the accused resides. If the accused travels to other States new warrants directed to those States have to be issued. It was for that reason that I have made a request to every Member State to inform the Tribunal of any information it receives concerning the travel plans of any person indicted by the Tribunal. In the cases of Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic, I might mention, relevant States have responded promptly and efficiently with that request. However, an international warrant of arrest issued pursuant to Rule 61 is directed to each and every Member State, and Interpol is requested to take efficient steps open to it to ensure that the accused person is arrested and surrendered for trial to the Tribunal. The effect of this, an international warrant, is to confine the accused to the State or area in which she or he is being given sanctuary. The accused effectively becomes an international fugitive. The publication of the evidence before the Tribunal and the issue of the international warrant of arrest have important deterrent effects. I dare say that no sane or rational person would wish to render himself or herself subject to such proceedings. In the future, would-be violators of international humanitarian law will know that such a fate may be in store for him or her and that knowledge may well stop or at least curb criminal suc conduct. Then, the evidence will constitute a permanent judicial record for all time of the horrendous war crimes that have been committed in the former Yugoslavia. That public record will assist in attributing guilt to individuals and be an important tool in avoiding the attribution of collective guilt to any nation or ethnic group. Some national truth commissions have been successful in fulfilling such a role by naming accused persons and revealing the evidence reasonably supporting their guilt. At the cost of repetition, your Honours, this is not a trial in absentia and the primary reason for the issue of an international warrant of arrest is to achieve the very objective of bringing the accused for trial. Indeed, these proceedings should be seen as an international challenge to the accused to come forward and either plead guilty or offer a defence before a legitimately established international criminal tribunal. That legitimacy was eloquently confirmed by the Appeal Chamber of this Tribunal in its historic judgment delivered at the beginning of last week. In that judgment the Appeal Judges stated, I quote: "It would be a travesty of law and a betrayal of the universal need for justice, should the concept of State sovereignty be allowed to be raised successfully against human rights. Borders should not be considered as a shield against the reach of the law and as protection for those who trample underfoot the most elementary rights of humanity. We continue to submit, that Rule 61 proceedings should convey to those harbouring suspected war criminals that such conduct is anathema to the international community and they should be seen as a plea, in the name of justice, to all Member States to do all in their power to place pressure on those responsible for protecting accused persons and to play their legal and moral role in ensuring that a proper trial be allowed to proceed. The fact that there is no accused sitting opposite me today is in no way the fault of the Prosecution and in no way a consequence of any defect in the Rules of Procedure of the Tribunal or, indeed, of the Statute. The success of these Rule 61 proceedings will depend upon the actions of Member States and the Security Council. I have laid much emphasis upon the rights of an accused and of the primary right to a trial in person. However, there can be no justification at all for ignoring the rights of the victims and of their families. They, too, have a right to be heard and thereby begin their own healing process and that of many tens of thousands of victims who will identify with them. The failure by the accused to come forward and stand trial and the complicity of any Member States or de facto administration should not be allowed effectively to close the mouths of those victims. For all of these reasons the Prosecution has invoked the provisions of Rule 61 in this, the Nikolic case, and it will do so in the future, should that become necessary. Your Honours, these proceedings which commence today are against Dragan Nikolic, also known as "Jenki" Nikolic The Prosecutor satisfied your Honour Judge Odio Benito that all reasonable steps had been taken to effect service of the warrant of arrest upon Nikolic and that the required newspaper advertisements had been published. Your Honour accordingly made the order pursuant to which we are assembled here today. Nikolic was the first person to be indicted by this Tribunal. That indictment was confirmed by your Honour Judge Odio Benito on 4th November 1994. According to information received by my Office, the absence of Nikolic cannot be ascribed to the fault of a Member State of the United Nations. Nikolic is presently residing in that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina which is under the de facto control of the Bosnian-Serb administration in Pale. The indictment alleges that about between 13th June and 30th September 1992, Nikolic was the commander of a camp called Susica. It was situated in the town of Vlasenica in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Nikolic is alleged to have participated in the murder of eight persons, the assault or torture of seven persons, and the unlawful confinement, transfer, persecution and inhumane treatment of some 500 innocent civilians in Vlasenica, and with having plundered or otherwise illegally misappropriated their property. 10 witnesses who were present at the relevant time in Vlasenica have with great courage decided to come to The Hague to testify in these proceedings. In full knowledge of their rights to witness protection they have further elected to give their evidence openly in public. Theirs will be the first voices of the victims to atrocities i the former Yugoslavia to testify before this International Criminal Tribunal and by so doing their voices will echo throughout the world. The nature of their evidence and that of other evidence that will be placed before your Honours will be described by Mr. Niemann who, with Ms. McHenry, will represent me in these proceedings. Your Honours, with your permission, I will ask Mr. Niemann now to proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, as touched upon by the Prosecutor, the decision that has to be made under Rule 61 is that if the Trial Chamber is satisfied on that evidence that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused has committed all or any of the crimes charged in the indictment it shall so determine. Your Honours, this is to be contrasted with what happens when an indictment is confirmed under Article 18(4) of the Statute, for in that case it is for the Prosecutor to decide that a prime facie case exists before he embarks upon preparing an indictment. Once the indictment is prepared by the Prosecutor, it is submitted to the confirming Judge in order for the confirming Judge to satisfy him or herself that the decision by the Prosecutor that a prime facie case exists is appropriate. Thus, the confirming Judge does not make a fresh determination on whether or not there is the prime facie case but, rather, tests the decision of the Prosecutor, in order to see that his decision is correct. As the primary determination prior to confirmation is by the Prosecutor, where reasonable minds could differ as to whether a prime facie case exists or not, emphasis, it is submitted, should be placed on the reasonableness or otherwise of the Prosecutor's determination. In dealing with the assessment of whether or not there are reasonable grounds for a belief, the evidence should be viewed in the light most favourable to the Prosecutor, all available inferences should be drawn in favour of the Prosecution and apparent inconsistencies are not called for to be resolved. As to the meaning of prime facie case, Rule 47 of the Rules of the Tribunal uses the phrase "... reasonable grounds for believing that a suspect has committed a crime within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal". These words were considered by His Honour Judge Sidwha on 29th August 1995 when confirming the indictment against Ivava Rajic, Case No. IT-95-12-1. At page 8 of his Honour's view, he said, I quote: "... the word reasonable is associated with what is fair, moderate, suitable, tolerable, that which is not immoderate or excessive. The expression 'reasonable grounds' is used; not overly convincing, substantial or conclusive grounds. Reasonable grounds, therefore, point to such facts and circumstances as would justify a reasonable or ordinary prudent man to believe that a suspect has committed a crime. To constitute reasonable grounds, facts must be such which are within the possession of the Prosecutor which raise a clear suspicion of the suspect being guilty of the crime. It predicates that all the ingredients of the offence are covered. The evaluation is to be made at the pretrial stage of the proceedings and not what may turn out subsequently in the light of changing facts. It is sufficient that the Prosecutor has acted with caution, impartiality and diligence, as a reasonably prudent Prosecutor would under the circumstances to ascertain the truth of his suspicions. It is not necessary this he has double-checked every piece of evidence, or investigated the crime personally, or instituted an enquiry in any special matter. It is sufficient that from an overall view of the evidence which he has collected and which covers all ingredients of the offence, including the necessary legal implications, which he seeks can be drawn therefrom, a clear suspicion of the accused being guilty of the crime arises. The evidence, therefore, need not be overly convincing or conclusive: it should be adequate and satisfactory to warrant the belief that the suspect has committed the crime. The expression 'sufficient evidence' is thus not synonymous with 'conclusive evidence' or 'evidence beyond reasonable doubt'. As stated earlier, the expression 'prime facie case' carries no universal meaning. Rule 47, therefore, neither raises the threshold or lowers it; it explains the requirement which the Prosecutor has to meet before filing an indictment and to what extent can be taken as laying down some guidance for the assessment of that expression". That is the end of the quote. If your Honours please, there is no basis for drawing any distinction between the test to be applied by the confirming Judge under Rule 47 and the test to be applied by this Chamber under Rule 61. Indeed, Rule 61(C) uses the same terms as appears in Rule 47(A), namely: "... reasonable grounds for believing that the accused has committed ... the crimes charged in the indictment". In our submission then, it is for this Chamber to look specifically at each of the counts of the indictment and apply the test that I have just spelt out. In the indictment we have charged the following offences under the Statute. Firstly, with the murders of Durmo Handzic; Asim Zildzic, Mevludin Hatunic; Rasid Ferhatbegovic; Dzevad Saric; Muharem Kolarevic; Zekic and Ismet Dedic. They have been charged under Articles 2(a); 3 and 5(a) of the Statute. With respect to Mevludin Hatunic and Ismet Dedic, we have charged in the alternative, Inhumane Treatment, Cruel Treatment and Inhumane Acts, contrary to Articles 2(b), 3 and 5(i) respectively in the Statute. Secondly, we have charged the accused with Inhumane Treatment, Cruel Treatment and Inhumane Acts against Galib Music contrary to Articles 2(b), 3 and 5(i) of the Statute. Thirdly, we have charged the accused with the Torture, causing Great Suffering, Cruel Treatment and Inhumane Acts against Fikret Arnout, contrary to Articles 2(b) and (c), 3, Articles 5(f) and (i) respectively of the Statute. Fourthly, with the Torture -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Excuse me. Do you mean by that amending the presentation of your indictment compared with the initial submission which was made to the Judges -- let me remind you -- that this was the first indictment and that it detailed on a victim by victim basis; it did not globally list the indictments in a global level. So, in the present situation, do you intend not changing the contents, as I understand you, but changing the form of the presentation of your indictment, or will it be the indictment as it was presented, I cannot remember which date, but I think it was some good time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It will be the indictment as was initially presented for confirmation to Your Honour Judge Odio Benito. What I am doing is, in effect, summarising the indictment but making specific reference to the charges themselves and the victims of those charges. Fourthly, with the Torture of Mubin Music, contrary to Articles 2(b), 3 and 5(f). Fifthly, with the Torture, causing Serious Injury, Cruel Treatment and Inhumane Acts against Suad Mahmutovic contrary to Articles 2(b) and (c), 3, 5(f) and (i) of the Statute. Sixthly, with causing Great Suffering, Cruel Treatment and Inhumane Acts against Sead Ambeskovic. Seventhly, with subjecting Redjo Cakisic to Inhumane Treatment. Eighthly, with causing Hansa Cakisic Great Suffering, Outrages Upon Personal Dignity and Inhumane Acts, contrary to articles 2(c), 3 and 5 of the Statute. Finally, with a series of general offences relating to the Wilful Confinement and illegal Imprisonment of civilians, the Appropriation and Plunder of their property, their unlawful Transfer and Persecution, contrary to Articles 2(d) and (), 3(e), 5(e), (h) nd (i) respectively. In respect of counts 4, 5, 6, 7, 18, 20 to 24, we have charged criminal responsibility under Article 7(3) of the Statute, and in the other counts our theory of liability is in accord with Article 7(1) of the Statute. In order for you to be satisfied that there is 'reasonable belief that the accused has committed the crime', there must be sufficient evidence to enable you to suspect that a crime has been committed. When examining the relevant issues, if your Honours please, it is necessary to look to the various ingredients of the offences under the Statute of the Tribunal. Dealing firstly with Article 2 of the Statute, this provision deals with the grave breach sections of the Geneva Conventions. It would appear that not all elements of these offences may have to be proved beyond reasonable doubt, but that issue does not, of course, arise in these proceedings. However, the components of those offences are that the victims of the crimes are persons protected by one or other of the Geneva Conventions of 1949; that the actions or omissions occurred during an armed conflict, or partial or total occupation, in which the law for international armed conflict applies, such that the conflict or occupation is governed by the Geneva Conventions of 12th August 1949. In dealing with specifically the subparagraphs of Article 2 and, firstly, with wilful killing under Article 2(A): The components of this offence consist of the need to show via the evidence that the victim is dead; that the death resulted from an unlawful act or omission by the accused, and that at the time of the act or omission the accused had the intent to kill or inflict grievous bodily harm upon the victim. Turning to paragraph B of Article 2 which deals with the crime of torture, the components of this offence are that the victim was intentionally and unlawfully subjected to the infliction of severe physical or mental pain or suffering by the accused or his subordinate; and that the pain or suffering was inflicted for any of the following reasons, namely, to obtain information, to punish the victim, for the purposes of intimidating or coercing the victim, or for any reason based on discrimination of any kind. It is necessary that the accused or his subordinate acted at the instigation of, or with the consent or acquiescence of, an official ora person acting in an official capacity. Also contained within paragraph (b) of Article 2 is the crime of inhumane treatment. In our submission, the components of that offence are that the accused or his subordinate committed a specified act or omission against the victim; that the accused or a subordinate intended to unlawfully impair the physical, intellectual or moral integrity of the victim or otherwise subject him or her to indignities, pain or suffering out of proportion to treatment expected of one human being to another; and that the physical, intellectual or moral integrity of the victim was impaired or the victim otherwise suffered indignities, pain or suffering. Under paragraph (c) of Article 2, there is contained provision relating to the crime of wilfully causing great suffering. In our submission, the elements of this offence that the accused committed a specified act upon the victim; that the accused ora subordinate committed an act or omission with the intent of unlawfully inflicting great suffering and that this great suffering was thereby inflicted. Under Article 2(c) also is contained the provision relating to causing serious injury to body or health. In our submission, again it is necessary to show that the accused committed the crime upon the victim and that the accused or subordinate thereby intentionally and unlawfully inflicted serious injury to the body or health of the victim. Dealing then, if your Honour pleases, with Article 2(d) of the Statute, dealing with appropriation of property: It is necessary for there to be some evidence that the accused wantonly and unlawfully destroyed and/or took, obtained or withheld real or personal property from the possession of the owner or any other person; that the person or property was protected under the Geneva Conventions; and that the taking or withholding by the accused was with the intent to deprive another person of the use and benefit of that property. If your Honour pleases, appropriation in this context may appropriately mean appropriation, the taking of property from its lawful owner with or without the intent to permanently deprive. Your Honours, dealing then with paragraph (g) of Article 2, unlawful deportation or forcible transfer, in our submission, the elements of this offence are that the accused or a subordinate unlawfully deported or forcibly transferred the victim from the territory where the victim was present to a place outside that territory. Finally, with paragraph (j) of Article 2 of the Statute, unlawful confinement of a civilian: In our submission, the ingredients of this charge are that the accused or a subordinate unlawfully held, confined or otherwise restrained the liberty of the victim; that the victim was a civilian; and that the restraint was effected without affording the victim the procedural and substantive protections prescribed in the above mentioned Conventions. Your Honours, in respect of Article 2, in our submission, they are appropriate factors that should be applied to the charges when considering whether a reasonable suspicion arises that those crimes have been committed. Now turning to Article 3 which has also been charged in the indictment that I outlined: Article 3 of the Statute deals with violations of the laws or customs of war. Article 3 States that the Tribunal shall have the power to prosecute persons violating the laws or customs of war and specifically states that the enumerated offences in paragraph (a) to (e) of that Article are not exhaustive. Accordingly, in our submission, at a minimum, in addition, Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions are also applied. Your Honours, the provisions of common Article 3 are not set out in the Statute, so I will read that provision out for the assistance of the Chamber. Article 3 provides that, "in the case of armed conflict not of an international character occurring in the territory of one of the High Contracting parties, each party to the conflict shall be bound to apply, as a minimum, the following provisions: (1 ) persons taking no active part in the hostilities, including members of armed forces who have laid down their arms and those placed hors de combat by sickness, wounds, detention, or any other cause, shall in the circumstances be treated humanly, without any adverse distinction founded on race, colour, religion or faith, sex, birth or wealth, or any similar criteria. To this end the following acts are and shall remain prohibited at any time and in any place whatsoever with respect to the above mentioned persons. (a) violence to life and person, in particular murder of any kinds, mutilation, cruel treatment and torture; (b) taking of hostages; (c) outrages upon personal dignity, in particular humiliating and degrading treatment; (d) the passing of sentences and the carrying out of executions without previous judgment pronounced by a regularly constituted court, affording all the judicial guarantees which are recognised as indispensable by civilised peoples". The common element of these charges is that the actual omissions occurred during an armed conflict either international, internal or both. If your Honour pleases, dealings specifically then with the provisions of Common Article 3, again we have the offences charged of murder. I will not proceed to recite all of the ingredients of those charges as most of them are common with the charges of murder under Article 2 of the Statute. However, there are additional elements such as that the victim was a non-combatant or hors de combat, that the death resulted from the unlawful act, which is a common element, and that the accused had the intent. With respect to the charge of cruel treatment under Common Article 3, apart from the common elements, it is necessary for there to be some evidence that the accused or a subordinate thereby intended to subject the victim to cruel treatment. Your Honours, the provision with respect to torture, apart from the common elements applicable to Common Article 3, remain the same as those that I have mentioned in relation to torture under Article 2. Again, outrages upon personal dignity: Apart from the common elements applicable to those charges, there is the element that the accused thereby intended to inflict upon the dignity of the victim or subject the victim to humiliating or degrading treatment. Finally, dealing with plunder under the Article of the Statute, paragraph (e) of the Statute of the Tribunal, it is necessary for the Prosecution to produce some evidence that the accused ora subordinate wasted, spoiled or appropriated certain public or private property; that the property belonged to another person and that there existed the intent to deprive; the acts were unlawful in that they were clearly not required by military necessity. That then leaves, if your Honour pleases, the final Article of the Statute of the Tribunal that has been charged in the indictment and that is Article 5 of the Statute. Article 5 of the Statute of the Tribunal deals with Crimes against Humanity. In our submission, the common element applicable to that charge is that the act or omission was part of a widespread and/or systematic attack directed against the civilian population, and that the accused knew or had reason to know that his acts were part of an attack upon the civilian population. Again there is then listed in the Crimes against Humanity provisions of Article 5 of the Statute the specific offences, the first being that of murder which has also been charged in the indictment. I submit that apart from the specific elements relevant to a crime against humanity, the elements of this offence are in common with murder as charged under Article 2(a) of the Statute or Common Article 3. The next provision that appears in relation to the indictment concerns imprisonment under paragraph (e) of Article 5 of the Statute. The relevant elements, in our submission, for consideration by your Honours in relation to this charge is that the accused or a subordinate held, confined or otherwise restrained the liberty of the victim, and that the restraint was effected without affording the procedural and substantive protections prescribed in the Fourth Geneva Convention of 1949. In addition, there is the charge of torture under Article 5(f) of the Statute of the Tribunal. In our submission, except for the specific elements applicable to a crime against humanity, those elements that I have mentioned in relation to Article 2(b) of the Statute have equal force and application to this provision. The next provision that has been charged under Article 5(h) is persecution on political, racial or religious grounds. In our submission, the relevant elements of that offence for consideration are that the accused committed this specified act against the victim; that the specified act or omission was intended by the accused to harass, cause suffering or otherwise discriminate against the victim based on political, racial or religious grounds. Finally, paragraph (i) of Article 5 deals with inhumane acts. In our submission, the elements of that offence are that the act or omission of the accused was unlawful and included, but was not limited to, one or other of the following acts, that he seized or detained victim with the intent to hold him as hostage; that an outrage upon the personal dignity of the victim by inflicting humiliating or degrading treatment; by sentencing and carrying out the sentence, or (d) by unlawful acts intended to impair the physical, intellectual or moral integrity of the victim or otherwise subject the victim to indignities, pain or suffering grossly out of proportion to the treatment expected of one human being from another. Those then, your Honours, are, in our submission, the elements of the offences for consideration when coming to the determination that you are called upon to do under Rule 61 of the rules of the Tribunal. I have briefly covered the final Articles of Articles 3 and 5 on the basis that they have common elements. Turning, your Honour, to the facts of this case, in our submission, the Opstina of Vlasenica -- "Opstina", in our submission, is a word applied to a municipal region or district in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- is located in Eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina, within which the town of Vlasenica is also located. It is about 50 kilometres from the Serbian border and about 120 kilometres north-east of Sarajevo. It is of strategic importance, being located between Belgrade, Sarajevo and Pale. ccording to figures in 1991, both the Opstina and the town had a majority Muslim population. Commencing in 1990, increasing nationalism and tension arose between the Serbian and Muslim populations Vlasenica. It was declared an autonomous region within the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in January 1992 by Serbians from Vlasenica and surrounding areas, and tensions continued to increase into the spring of 1992 with the referendum on the proposed independence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. About 21st April 1994, the town of Vlasenica was forcibly taken over and declared to be a Serbian town. The Federal Army of Yugoslavia, referred to as the JNA soldiers, including soldiers from the Novi Sad corps from Serbian, paramilitary forces and local military soldiers occupied the area without any armed resistance from the Muslim population. Military matters were subsequently transferred from the JNA forces to the local Serbian forces which came about by the mobilisation of local Serbian men. When I say "Serbian", I am referring there the Bosnian-Serbian men. The community affairs which were prior to the takeover were largely managed by a committee comprising both Muslims and Serbs was now comprised only by Bosnian Serbs, and the Serbians were appointed to all the positions within the town. Conditions for Muslims deteriorated in such ways as terminations of employment, restrictions on travel and the withdrawal of funds and frequent arrests with police interrogations of Muslim men often accompanied by beatings, resulting in many Muslims fleeing the Vlasenica area. Between May 1992 and September 1992 the remaining Muslim population were either forcibly expelled or arrested, leaving virtually no Muslims in this area. Arrested Muslims were first held at a local school or the local prison before the setting up of a camp at Susica, run by the military and local militia. There were always at 500 detainees in the Susica camp and as many as 8,000 persons may have passed through this camp. The camp had two main buildings to house the detainees and a small house used for interrogations. The detainee hall was severely overcrowded, no sleeping material was provided, toilet facilities were limited and there were no showers. Beatings were common and the detainees lived in a state of constant fear. From at least mid June 1992, the commander of the camp was Dragan Nikolic, also known as "Jenki" Nikolic, who commanded the 12 soldiers guarding the detainees. Nikolic gave orders such as not allowing any persons to escape, not allowing other persons into the camp to carry out personal vendettas, and not allowing any of the prisoners to be taken from the camp without his approval and of obtaining a signed document. The witnesses will allege that Nikolic, as commander of the camp, was responsible for charges brought against him as detailed in the indictment that I have already outlined to your Honours. To assist your Honours, we have prepared on the video monitor a computer representation of maps relating to, firstly, Europe and then subsequently progressing down to the area of Vlasenica itself. With your Honours leave, I will ask Mr. Dixon to firstly display on the computer monitor a map of Europe which will indicate the location of, firstly, Yugoslavia. If your Honours please, if you press the button on the computer monitor on your consoles you should then be able to see this map shown. Perhaps, your Honour, while that is being prepared, I will continue and then come back to that. Your Honour, it is the intention of the Prosecution to call a total of 15 witnesses; the first witness will be Dr. James Gow, a Political Scientist, from the Department of War Studies, King's College, London, and a research associate from the Centre of Defence Studies, University of London. Your Honour, although technically the non-disclosure order that your Honours have made applies equally to Dr. Gow, as he is a Prosecution witness, we will be asking -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] We now have the map on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I will turn to the map. Your Honour, this is just a general map to show you the location of Yugoslavia in Europe. I will ask that we now be shown a map of Yugoslavia itself. Dr. Gow will go into greater detail of this area, but I merely show how Yugoslavia prior to its breakup and still exists in relation to its various borders. Perhaps the next map might be shown? Your Honours, this is a map of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The divisions that one can see on that map indicate the various Opstinas of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Might we focus in more directly on the Opstina of Valsenica? As described by your Honours, where the cursor now appears, your Honours, you can see Valsenica. As I mentioned in my address, it is relatively close to the border with the Republic of Serbia. Your Honour, what we have now displayed on the technical vision screen is a larger map concentrating more on the town of Vlasenica, but showing the town's location in the Opstina itself and a number of the towns surrounding the town of Valsenica which maybe referred to from time to time in the evidence of the witnesses. Finally, your Honours, we have a map or a plan of the city of Valsenica itself. Perhaps we could focus in a little closer? This map will also be referred to from time to time and details the town itself of Valsenica and will feature in the evidence of the witnesses and may also be referred to by Dr. Gow. Your Honours, following the calling of Dr. Gow who, I have said, we would be seeking a lifting of the non-disclosure order in relation to, we will then seek to call some 13 witnesses who are eyewitnesses to the events that occurred in the Opstina of Valsenica at the relevant period and, in particular, to what occurred to them at the Susica camp. We will then conclude with the evidence of Mr. Paepen, an investigator from the Investigation Section of the Office of the Prosecutor. Mr. Paepen is also affected by the non-disclosure order in relation to witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] What was the name of the last witnesses -- I did not quite catch it -- the last of the named witnesses you mentioned? M R. NIEMANN: It is "Paepen".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This witness, if your Honours pleases, is a summary witness in a sense. He will speak generally to the supporting statements and additional material that will be provided by the Prosecutor in relation to these proceedings. With respect to the 13 eyewitnesses, these witnesses will give their evidence in the Bosnian language which will be translated simultaneously into the French and English languages. By and large, these witnesses are unfamiliar with the judicial process of this Tribunal. Some of them are the victims of the crime and, as such, suffer trauma from their experience. The translation of one language to another language can cause some discrepancies to occur, especially when a word or concept in one language has no equivalent in the other. If your Honours please, we have for the assistance of the Chamber been provided with a very useful document by the translation unit which deals with some of the difficulties that can be encountered in the process of translation. With your Honours' leave, in due course I will tender or submit that to your Honours for your assistance. Finally, your Honours, as you have seen, we would hope and intend to make use of the various visual aids available in the courtroom. The lay witnesses are not familiar with the use of these devices, although they have been given a demonstration on how they might work. But it may occur that from time to time they may become confused or uncertain about these devices. We would ask the court to be patient with these witnesses if we encounter difficulties of this nature. Your Honour, I now wish to call the evidence. Firstly, I would ask that the non-disclosure order in relation to the first witness be lifted. This witness is not a victim witness. He is an expert witness. He does not wish that his name be suppressed or any other matters relating to his identity be non-disclosed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] I would like to explain the situation. This is covered by an order of non-disclosure. Furthermore, the Chamber has taken steps to restrict the number of disclosures made, so we have a public character which is the ultimate aim of the Rule 61 hearing, except for specific measures to be undertaken for the witnesses themselves who, very frequently are the victims. So they are aware of what is going on, so that each witness knows what is going on, and we will have to review it on an individual basis. So, the order taken by the Chamber some days ago means that the identity, the addresses and all the elements of identification are not revealed, unless that particular person wishes the contrary. That is the current state of affairs. Bearing that in mind, this will not be applied to the first witness who will be mentioned as Mr. Niemann has explained to us. That is why for this particular witness the identity of the witness can be disclosed. I ask the court, therefore, to take note of that and include it in our record.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If the Chamber pleases, I call Andrew James William Gow.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Mr. James Gow, on the basis of an order you can provide us with your identification and then make the solemn declaration to the court. I think somebody will be giving you a text of the solemn declaration. That has already been carried out, Registrar, so if you could introduce yourself, tell us who you are, pronounce the solemn declaration standing, then you can sit down and begin your testimony. Of course, be ready to answer questions which the court may ask you or by the Office of the Prosecutor. So the floor is yours. ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW, Sworn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Andrew James William Gow. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Thank you very much. The Registrar has noted this declaration. You may sit down. Mr. Gow, please begin your statement as you wish to in order to help us in administering justice and in order to help the Tribunal understand what has been happening. The floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, are you a political scientist with the positions of Lecturer in the Department of War Studies, King's College, London, and a Research Associate of the Centre for Defence Studies, University of London?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Formally, were you a Research Officer at the Centre for Defence Studies and before that Lecturer on Soviet and Eastern European Affairs at Hatfield Polytechnic in the United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you hold the Degree of PhD from the University of London where you prepared your doctorial thesis on Yugoslavia at the school of Slovonic and Eastern European Studies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the past several years has your work been concentrated on former Yugoslavia, particularly its military-political affairs and have you written and lectured extensively about this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is fair to say that is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your evidence based upon your personal knowledge drawn from your own work and that of other recognised scholars in this field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you published reports, military and civilian writings, speeches and other official documents from the area of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you published reports, military and civilian writings, speeches and other documents from the area of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have published work which is based on materials of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you also based your research on conversations with knowledgeable persons and witness statements and documents made available to you by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since 1988 have you published numerous books and articles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are the details of those books, monographs, articles and other writings that you have published been presented in a statement that was made available to the confirming Judge in relation to the presentation of this indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, concerning the former Republic of Yugoslavia, can you tell the court about the political composition of the former Yugoslavia prior to 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia was a federation of six republics, Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina -- Bosnia and Herzegovina comprising two historic areas, Bosnia and Herzegovina -- Montenegro, Serbia and Macedonia. There were also two autonomous provinces which had a high degree of autonomy in place, certain roles at the Federal level, both within Serbia, Kosovo and Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber about the ethnic composition of Yugoslavia prior to 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ethnic composition of Yugoslavia was a complex mix of populations. The largest population groups were the Serbs, the Croats, the Slav Muslims in Bosnia and in Serbia, the Slovenes, the Macedonians, Montenegrins and also the non-Slav Albanians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at this document that I now show to you please? (Handed). What does that document represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document represents information on proportions within the population of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia -- if I may say, the SFRY for brevity -- in that as reflected in the censuses taken in 1981 and 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From where is it compiled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is compiled from the census data as presented in a memorandum from the United Kingdom Foreign and Commonwealth Office to the Houses of Parliament, Foreign Affairs Committee in London.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who prepared the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This particular document was prepared at my direction for the purposes of Offices of the Prosecutor -- Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With your Honours' leave, might I ask Mr. Dixon to assist the witness in displaying this particular document on the video display unit so that the witness may explain the document to your Honours? Your Honours, in order to pick up this, you will need to press the videoing monitor button on your Honours' consoles. (To the witness): Dr. Gow, dealing specifically with the document on the machine, can you just take the court through the document and explain it in relation to your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document shows the share of population of the most significant groups in the SFRY. I should correct the information presented here and note that Montenegrins are missing. The document shows that the single largest group through the territories of the SFRY were the Serbs; that they constituted a little over a third of the population as a whole. So, as the single largest group, they did not form an absolute majority. It goes on to show the proportions of other populations within the SFRY as a whole. It shows that in the period of 10 years between the 1981 and 1991 census there were some small changes but the population levels remained fairly stable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In addition to the populations presented in this table of information, there were, of course, some other smaller groups which do not feature, adding to the very complex mix of populations that were to be found within Yugoslavia. It should be noted that all population groups were found in all -- were found in more than one republic, although, of course, there were concentrations of Serbs in Serbia, Croats in Croatia, Slovenes in Slovenia and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that document for the record, your Honours. May it be handed to the court? (To the witness): Would you now look at the next document that will be shown to you by Mr. Dixon? Just perhaps show the witness the document, if you would, please? Firstly, do you know what this document is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document shows the single largest group within the population of each of the six republics which comprise the SFRY, and it shows the percentage proportion of the population that the largest group represented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It has not been displayed as yet, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Excuse me, Mr. Niemann, I think we have been given the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. For the record, I seek to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] You wish to tender that document, fine. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): The document you have in front of you, who compiled that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The information is based on the results of the 1981 census taken throughout the territories of the SFRY. It was in the present form derived from information submitted in a memorandum from the United Kingdom Foreign and Commonwealth Office to the House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee in London.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you place the document on the video recording machine, please? By specific reference to it, can you explain the document to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document shows the single largest group within each of the six republics of the SFRY. You will note that only in Slovenia was there something that could be described as real ethnic homogeneity, that in all other places, although there was a single largest group, there were large -- other large, a large share of the population was formed by one or more other groups. You will note that whereas in Croatia, Montenegro and Macedonia there was an absolute majority of the naming group, in Serbia also that was the case, although the proportion within what is known as "narrow Serbia" rose significantly from 66.4 per cent of Serbia as a whole, including the two autonomous provinces, to 85.4 per cent of Serbs within Serbian -- Serbia proper. You will also note that in Bosnia, although the Muslims constituted the single largest group, they were not an absolute majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender that document for the record. Dr. Gow ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Mr. Prosecutor, it is now quarter past 11. I do not want to interrupt the witness making a statement, so do you have a question which would be an overall summary of the statement or would you like to take a break at this point? Would you like to raise a question which would just take a couple of minutes or so to answer? We do not have to stop at 11.15 on the dot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, I have one question which I think can conclude the witness's evidence at this stage. (To the witness): Dr. Gow, had by 1991 the ethnic composition of the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina altered at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The evidence of the 1991 census in Bosnia and Herzegovina showed that the proportion of Muslims within the population had increased from approximately 39 per cent to around 44 per cent; that the proportion of Serbs had decreased to 31.5 per cent and that the figure for Croats was 17 per cent. So, although there remained stability within, more or less stability within the levels of populations, there were noticeable growths in the case of the Muslims and reductions in the case of Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient time to adjourn, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Yes, quite. Thank you very much. We will come back and continue the testimony from Dr. Gow at 11.30. The session is adjourned. (Short Adjournment) (11.30 a.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Before giving the floor to our witness, Dr. Gow, I would like to make some comments: I am somewhat concerned that we follow closely and that our work runs smoothly. It seems to me that, on a technical point of view, sometimes we have some hiccups, but I also want to look at the Prosecutor's Office and tell them that the interpreters are facing some difficulties to follow you and that is for two reasons. The first reason is that they do not have sufficient documentation, and since our interpreters, just like all of us, are in a situation of stress, I think it would be very sound management to provide them the maximum of documentation. It will assist the court, it will also assist all the legal participants and also, since it is a public hearing, since the media is following us closely, it is good to provide all the instruments possible to have good, reliable interpretation. If the documents are not available, perhaps, Mr. Niemann, if you could perhaps speak at a slightly slower pace, not quite so impetuous. Even although I know it is because you are moved by your personal conviction, it would be appreciated if you would be more moderate in your tone. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will do what I can, your Honour, to assist the interpreters. I understand a copy of the statement of Dr. Gow has been available to the interpreters. I hope that is so; if it is not, I will take steps to correct it. (To the witness): Dr. Gow, prior to the adjournment, you were giving your evidence about the various ethnic groups in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. Can you tell the Chamber what languages the various ethnic groups speak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The main language on the territories of the SFRY was commonly known as Serbo-Croat. Today, it is frequently called either Croatian, Bosnian, Serbian, even Montenegrin. That language was spoken by around 80 per cent of the population on the territories of the SFRY. It was a Slovenic language; it was a language in which there were some regional variations but which was, essentially, as far as I understand, linguists look at it the same language. Slovenes and Macedonians spoke Slovonic languages that were distinct but related to Serbo-Croat, and a number of other populations, the smaller groups, spoke other languages. For example, the large Albanian minority spoke Albanian and the Hungarians in Vojvodina in the north spoke Hungarian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, was there any variations in the religious beliefs of the various ethnic groups in the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The main religions in the area were Roman Catholicism which was embraced predominantly by the Slovenes and Croats; Eastern Orthodoxy, embraced by the Christian populations mostly who were living on the eastern side of a divide in the -- the Serbs, the Montenegrins the Macedonians, and Islam which was adhered to by the Slav Muslims in Bosnia and in Serbia, as well as Islam adhered to by the non-Slavs, that is, the Albanians in the largely Albanian populated area of Kosovo. I might also add that there were Albanians in Montenegro but many of these embraced Roman Catholicism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, you mentioned something earlier in your evidence about the population distribution of Yugoslavia. Specifically in relation to Yugoslavia, in Bosnia in particular, has there been any variations in this population distribution since 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The events since 1991 have given rise to substantial movements in the population and the population structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Estimates vary, and they run up to around 3.7 million people having been disturbed and forcibly -- and displaced either forcibly or as refugees from the places in which they lived in 1991 and before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at this document that I now show you? (Handed). Could you just describe what that document is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is a table which identifies regions within Bosnia and Herzegovina. It gives a breakdown of the different population groups within each of those areas, and it shows the absolute figures based on the 1991 census for the share of population in that area in 1991 and, finally, shows figures for the summer of 1994 and, in putting the two sets of figures together, gives us some indication of the changes which have taken place in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who prepared the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is based on information from the 1991 census throughout the territories of the SFRY with application in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and on information provided by the United Nations High Commissioner for refugees. It was prepared in this form at my direction for the purposes of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you now place a copy of that document on the screen? Your Honours, I have a copy here for your Honours to refer to in case your Honours have difficulty in seeing the one displayed on the screen. (To the witness): Dr. Gow, just dealing with the schedule that you have there, can you describe the schedule as it has been presented there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The schedule shows the population changes since 1991. If you were to look at the first column, you will see certain regions identified. The second column shows the breakdown of ethnic groups within those regions, in each case Croat and Muslim with the exception of figures compiled by the UNHCR for the safe areas designated in Eastern Bosnia of Srebrenica, Gorazde and Zepa at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps a little bit slower, I think. The column, the third column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The third column shows the absolute figures in the population in those areas based on the 1991 census. The final figure shows figures derived from the UNHCR for the situation in July 1994. The figures reveal, if you look, the changes in the composition of the population in each of those areas. As one example, you may look at the first identified region, Western Bosnia, you will note that in 1991, according to the census, there were approximately 300,000 non-Serbs living in that area, but by July 1994 the combined total for non-Serbs was estimated to be 10,000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That then continues throughout the schedule in relation to, for example, there is Srebrenica, you have a ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For Srebrenica, you have almost -- if I may?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For Srebrenica you get a reflection of the same kind of change but, perhaps, in an opposite direction you note that the Serb share of the population was almost 80,000 in 1991, but by July 1994 this had been reduced to about a quarter of that -- of what it had been in 1991. Conversely, the Muslim population had grown by around 100,000 reflecting an influx of populations from other areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The opposite effect can be seen when looking at the Muslim population in Northern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Muslim population in Northern Bosnia again, as in the first case I noted as an example of Western Bosnia, shows a substantial reduction in the number of Muslims in the population in that area from 355,000 in 1991 down to approximately 40,000 in 1994. The same goes for the Croat share of the population, 180,000 in 1991, 30,000 in 1994. At the same time you will note a slight increase in this particular area of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that document. (To the witness): Dr. Gow, I would like you now to turn to the historical political background of the former Yugoslavia. When was Yugoslavia first proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yugoslavia was proclaimed on 1st December 1918 as the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What followed after that proclamation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The newly formed state was consolidated over a period of three years and was finally settled with a constitution established on 28th June 1921.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. From what was the word "Yugoslav" derived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The word "Yugoslav" is derived from the Serbo-Croat word "jug" meaning "south" and the word "slav" describing the particular type of people. It, therefore, means South Slavs or the land of the South Slavs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was sought to be achieved by the formation of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The formation of Yugoslavia represented the possibility of achieving or accomplishing in reality two ideas which had developed in the 19th century. One was the idea that the Serbs living on Ottoman and former Ottoman territories should all be able to live together spread throughout the region as they were; the other idea developed by intellectuals in the Austro-Hungarian Empire was that the Yugoslavs, the south Slavs, all shared common features and should be able to live together in a manifestation of something which we might call self-determination. If I may make a point of explanation at this stage in case it is not clear to your Honours, that for much of this period in history, Yugoslavia, the lands which went to make up Yugoslavia, were divided between two empires; on the North and Western side the Austro-Hungarian Habsburg Empire, and on the Eastern side the Islamic or Turkish Ottoman Empire, and that this division was made by the borders between Croatia and Bosnia until 1878, at which point Austria annexed Bosnia and Herzegovina, and so the border between Bosnia and Serbia became the border between the empires. I think it is quite important maybe as a point as an explanation for what I just said to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] The wonderful maps which shown us, would it be, perhaps, possible to have them? You know the maps you showed us on Yugoslavia? R. NIEMANN: Yes, your Honour. PRESIDING JUDGE: [Original in French] Could we have perhaps a copy we could follow more closely the statements made by Dr. Gow? NIEMANN: Yes, your Honour. Your Honour, I will just enquire as to whether we have a number of copies of those maps. I know that we have one copy, but whether we have more than one, I am not sure. If your Honours excuse me for a moment?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, what are the major geographical and topographical features of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As diverse as Yugoslavia was in terms of its population, it was also diverse in terms of geophysical features. In the north eastern part, the north eastern and eastern parts of the country there were large plains of the region -- there still are large plains. There are two distinction mountainous regions, one, the alpine region in the north in Slovenia, another in the central areas of Bosnia and Croatia and, of course, there was the Dalmatian coast line with its particular features. These particular features are important in terms of understanding, perhaps, some of the historical divide I just mentioned. The division between the empires included the coast line and the flat lands on either side, and the division came through the mountainous areas reflecting possibilities of defence and border land confrontation between the two empires.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, flowing from that, would you say that the geographical nature of Yugoslavia has had an impact upon its historical and cultural development?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I would say that. Although, of course, anything like that will always be a combination of features, it is clear that the geography of Yugoslavia has underpinned some of the divisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the impact of these geographical and cultural and historical features more pronounced in any one particular area of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is fair to say that in Bosnia and Herzegovina the complexities manifest in Yugoslavia as a whole in the coming together of these various features were more pronounced. They were more pronounced in part because of the creation of mountains and valleys, people mixing and not mixing, but also because Bosnia and Herzegovina was the area which was transferred from one of the empires, the Austro-Hungarian, to the other in 1878. So, the mix of populations reflected the ancient division between the two halves of the Christian church, Roman Catholicism and the Eastern Orthodox church. It then went on to represent the division between Western Roman Catholic Christianity and the Islamic Turkish Empire, meaning that population in the area might be Roman Catholic by religion, might be Eastern Orthodox by religion, or might be Islamic by religion; these factors being overlaid by the history of warfare and the shifting lines between the empires.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, against this background of diversity that you have explained in your evidence, where then did the concept of Yugoslavia come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, as I indicated before, the idea of Yugoslavia emerged as such among South Slav intellectuals in the Austro-Hungarian empire. It was the idea that all South Slav people speaking either the same language or a closely related language should be able to live together and gain some sense of common existence, a way of self-expression, self-determination. At the same time an alternative view of Yugoslavia was that put forward often called "Great Serbia", one in which all these people would live together because either most of them were Serbs in the eyes of certain thinkers in the 19th century, or because most of the Serbs would be in the area and the others would be able to live together with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, what, if any, impact did World War I have on the formation of the Yugoslav State?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The outcome of World War I was quite important in the formation of the Yugoslav State. As I just said, there were these two ideas which had been around in the previous century developing, but the formation of Yugoslavia in the way that it was formed was very much a product of the end of the First World War. A little bit of the history is important. In 1915, Serbia was one of the allies of the Western powers. The allied powers and Serbia was fighting the war with the idea that it would be able to create this Yugoslav or great Serbian State at the end of war. In 1915, the allied powers induced Italy to join with them in the fight and, in doing so, offered them territories which would later become part of Slovenia and Croatia. At the end of the First World War, when the allied powers were victorious over the central powers and the allied powers had clearly decided that the Austro-Hungarian Empire should be broken up, the South Slavs were in a position of some weakness -- the South Slavs from the Habsburg Empire were in a position of some weakness, facing an Italian threat to -- parts of this area had already been annexed and Italy looking to take the other territories. So they decided to form a common State with the Serbs at that stage, and one in which they had largely to accept Serbian terms for unification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the major political developments or events in Yugoslavia between World War I and World War II?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The formation of this first Yugoslav State was not cemented until the constitution was put in place in 1921, on 28th June. That constitution was more or less an extension of the pre-existing Serbian monarchy. It was a constitutional monarchy under the Serbian king. It was a State in which many non-Serbs felt they did not have a real stake. Therefore, the next 20 years were characterised by political nationalist, economic crises of various kinds and the State became politically weak and unviable. So that in 1929 King Alexander declared a Royal State of emergency. He renamed the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, but with this period of a state of emergency became even more unpopular with some of the non-Serbs leading to his assassination by a team of Macedonian and Croat nationalists in 1934. At the end of the 1930s Yugoslavia was politically, socially, economically weak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the main features of World War II in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The weakness of this first Yugoslav State meant that when in April 1941 the axis powers invaded it was easy for them to occupy the territory as a whole and to dismember it, breaking it up into different areas. In one of those areas they installed a puppet regime, the Ustasha regime, in the so-called independent State of Croatia. The Ustasha were one of the three main groups to fight the Second World War on the territories of Yugoslavia. The other two groups were the pro-Serbian Royalist Chetniks, loyal to the old King and to the old Serbian army, and the partisans led by communists under the leadership of Yosiv Ros Tito. The main features of this war, which was part a revolution, part a civil war and part a war of national liberation, were that the ethnic exclusivity, and particularly the vicious anti-Serbian campaign of the Ustasha, meant that many people would turn to the partisans who were better organised, who appeared to offer something to everybody without being nationally exclusivist for the future, and began to offer protection to the Serbs against the Ustasha at the same time as they could offer a future in which all the other Yugoslav peoples would be able to have a stake. They promoted the idea of regional or what would become republican government within a Federal structure, thereby giving the non-Serbs the idea that they would have a stake in their place in the new Federal State.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who emerged from World War II as this successful party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The partisans emerged as the victors in World War II and were able to establish a federation under communist -- a federation with this structure of six republics, but under Communist rule under the leadership of Tito.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the Communists go about the task of taking control of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The process I alluded to a moment ago of offering the various groups a stake in the future, promoting the idea of the Federal structure, began to be elaborated from 1943 onwards when the partisans began to institute local administrations, regional councils on areas under their control, areas liberated from the control of either their opponents or of the axis occupiers. This became the underpinning for the Federal system which was put in place after the war, making some appeal to all the people, giving all the people some sense that they had their own little bit, their own State within a State which would become part a new Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the federation? It was a Federation of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Federation was established formally in 1946 as the Federal Peoples Republic of Yugoslavia. It was a Federation of six republics. The two autonomous provinces at that stage were identified, but had little formal power. The Federation established of the six republics was under Communist rule, and I think it would be fair to say that the Communists, whilst selling the idea of the Federation, never really intended that it should have meaning in reality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just remind us again, the name of the two provinces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The two provinces established within Serbia were Vojvodina in the North and Kosovo in the South.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did the constitutional model of the first Communist Yugoslavia State come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Federal model for the constitution was adopted from that present in the Soviet Union. It was similar in structure; a mixture of different population groups formed into what were designated as sovereign republics constituting a Federation when they joined together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the relationship between Yugoslavia and the Soviet Union, what was the nature of that relationship between Yugoslavia and the Soviet Union immediately following World War II?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The relationship between Yugoslavia and the Soviet Union at the end of World War II was very good. The Yugoslav Communists were very keen to emulate what the Soviets had been doing and established very close links with them. However, between 1945 and 1948 the initial enthusiasm gave way to a series of tensions and disputes with the result that by 1948 Stalin, the Soviet Ruler at the time, decided to expel Yugoslavia from the bloc of Communist movements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the implication of this expulsion by the Soviet Union of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the biggest implication was that the Yugoslav Communists had to protect themselves, and to protect themselves they had to justify the split and in justifying the split they had to prove they were different from and better than the Soviets; that meant they had to find an alternative Communist model. They went away and came up with the idea of socialist self-management. It is important to understand that this idea contained large elements of decentralisation, and it was the move to a model in which there was decentralisation which began to give the Federal structure of the different republics real meaning within the Yugoslav framework.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you have said, is it true to say that there was a centralising force and corresponding decentralising force in the nature of the Federation of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would indeed be fair to say that. It is in the nature of Communist rule to centralise authority, but at the same time it is quite clear that when you begin to decentralise a tension will emerge between the centripetal forces and the centrifugal forces, a tension between the centre wanting to draw power into itself and the periphery wanting to accrue power and be protected from the centre. I think it would be fair to say that much of the history of Yugoslavia over the next 40 years could be characterised in terms of the struggle between centralising forces and decentralising forces in debates of political, social, economic policy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "next 40 years", you are speaking from World War II up to the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
