utterances.text: I am speaking approximately from the split with the Soviets in 1948 through to 1988, approximately at the end of the 1980s when the final dissolution, the period of final dissolution I think began.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made reference to Tito earlier in your evidence. What role did Tito play in the Federal system that was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the wartime leader Tito played an extremely important role. He had immense personal authority within this structure of Federal elements, both Communist party elements and administrative elements. In the period of 40 years I was describing, through much of that period although there was tension between the centre and the republics, it was also clear that Tito could use his personal authority to resolve differences between the republics, to keep differences at a less than critical level and to provide the way for compromise. I think when Tito died in 1980 an important factor was taken away. He had been appointed President for life, everybody approved of that; without Tito it became increasingly difficult to find compromises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the major developments in the constitutional evolution of Communist Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Communist Yugoslavia had four separate constitutions each reflecting gradually this process of decentralisation of power. The first in 1946 was based on the Soviet model, as I said, and was highly centralised. The second in 1953, I think, reflected the introduction of the idea of socialist self-management and increased decentralisation. That proved to be inadequate for the circumstances, as through the 1950s and into the early 1960s the debates we described between centre and republics continued, and so a further constitution was adopted in 1963, again enhancing the role of the republics. The final constitution was adopted in 1974. At that point the country was renamed the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and that constitution essentially confirmed the arrangement which had emerged in reality in which the republics acted in a quasi-confederal way, each with its own spheres of power and very few powers remaining with the Federation. It was important, as I said before, to note in that structure the role of Tito as President for life because he was able to regulate differences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were these features reflected in the 1974 constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The essential features reflected in the 1974 constitution were the right to self-determination of the peoples of Yugoslavia, including the right to secession; the limitation on that right that it would require agreement of the different peoples, that there would be a distinction between what were called "peoples" or "nations", that is the State forming peoples who did not have another homeland somewhere else and what were called "nationalities" or "national minorities", those people for whom there would be a homeland somewhere else. If I may give one example, for the Serbs Yugoslavia, as it was, constituted the only homeland; for Hungarians within Serbia within Yugoslavia, of course, Hungary provided another homeland. Therefore, they would have this status of national minorities. Finally and most importantly, in my opinion, the constitution established clearly the identification of the republics as States with sovereign rights, and made the distinction between the republics as States with sovereign rights and the provinces which did not have that status.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us the name of those States again? I know you have said it earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am glad to. These were Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Montenegro and Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the two provinces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The two provinces within Serbia, Vojvodina and Kosovo. I might also add, if I may, that in the 1974 constitution although they were given a different status, the real power of those two autonomous provinces were significantly increased.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the political ramifications of this 1974 constitution that you have spoken of following Tito's death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I indicated, while Tito was there he could regulate the differences between the republics. After Tito died through the 1980s it became increasingly impossible for the various republics to agree. There was a growing political, social, economic and constitutional crisis. Various ideas emerged for solutions to that crisis but of course, as you may guess, the ideas were somewhat polarised. The polarisation of ideas was reflected within particular republics within the SFRY, and by the end of 1980s it was becoming very difficult to see a prospect for common agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What republic was the first republic to react as a consequence of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first republic to address the question of the 1974 constitution and to raise the question of asserting its own sovereignty, was the republic of Serbia. It did so following a memorandum published by the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences in 1985 in which the proposition was put that Serbia had been a victim of Tito's Yugoslavia, that it had been unfairly treated, that it was a matter of injustice that only Serbia had these two autonomous provinces limiting its formal sovereignty, that is as a sovereign State it was in some sense curtailed in the scope of its powers by the existence of these two provinces, and that Serbia should reassert its sovereignty first over the provinces and then within the Federation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Concentrating more on this break-up process of Yugoslavia, what steps ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Mr. Niemann, I would like to ask two brief questions of the witness before we continue discussion of dissolution. The first question is this. The founding peoples Slovenes, Croatians, the founding peoples seem apparently all to have had a territory: Slovenia, Croatia, etc. What about the Muslims? Were they considered as being Bosnians? Was it considered that the Muslims were a founding people of the territory which corresponds to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When Bosnia and Herzegovina was established at the end of the Second World War, it was established within the borders of an historical territory, the territory which had been part of the Ottoman empire, then part of the Austro-Hungarian empire. The formation of that republic was based largely on the historical identity of a State or a territory in which historically there had been three separate populations: the Slav Muslim, the orthodox Serbs and the Roman Catholic Croats. At that time, although there was some discussion of the Slav Muslims being sent to constitute a State forming people, they were not regarded as a State forming people. It was not until the 1960s that they were formally given the status of a State forming people within the SFRY, and from that time onwards they were regarded as being a State form people within SFRY and within Bosnia and Herzegovina, but they were not the exclusive, not the only State-forming people within Bosnia and Herzegovina I think it would be fair to say. Is that sufficient?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Thank you very much, Dr. Gow. The second question before we go over to the separation process, it is an historical question by the way, I would like to now ask you, at a particular point in time was there a specific expression given to the idea of a concrete idea of Serbia or did it remain a type of mythology for the founding peoples?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: : There have been various expressions of the idea of a Great Serbia. The idea originally emanated in the thinking of Ilija Garasanin, a Minister in the developing independent Serbian State in the 19th century, and that was the idea that all the territories inhabited by orthodox populations should be incorporated within a State. The line usually associated with this idea of Great Serbia later given definition by others is the line running along the axis Karlobag, Karlovac and Virovitica. This is a line running from the Dalmatian coast through parts of Croatia to the border between Croatia and Hungary. Would that be an adequate answer?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Yes, very largely. So, there was no concrete expression given, historically speaking, to the idea of Great Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: : May I ask what would constitute a concrete expression? I think the idea of the line drawn between Karlobag, Karlovac and Virovitica, these three towns, is the line which would designate the concrete expression of a Great Serbia which would include the lands otherwise between present -- between the then Serbia, and including the territory of Serbia as it is now, the lands of Macedonia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and those parts of Croatia which would fall within the line on the map. If your Honour wishes, I could possibly indicate, if I were given a copy of a map, I could possibly indicate where this line would run?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps that map could be brought up on to the computer screen, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] What I meant by my question was a political concrete expression. So, in actual fact, in political terms, there was never any Great Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: : In political terms, an entity called "Great Serbia" never existed. It was only ever an idea and a plan. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Just looking at the plan that now appears on the television screen, are you able to expand upon your answer to His Honour's question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if I could ask for the indicator to be moved to the Adriatic Coast first? Could you move it along the coast line, please, back a little bit. From a point approximately here, running across, if you would move across and move towards -- if you could go back to the coast and hold it there for a moment, if you can move the indicator first across the sea between the "C" and "R" of Croatia and then through to the Hungarian border near the "B" of Zagreb? That would be approximately the line which the map of Great Serbia envisaged -- that would be the border established under the historic idea of a Great Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to know, Dr. Gow, the role played by the Muslims during the Second War; did they support one specific side in that war or were they neutral? What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that they could be said to be neutral, but they did not support one specific side. There were Muslims who were formed by the axis powers into something called the Sandzak division, one of the auxiliaries of the axis powers. There were Muslims who fought with the partisans. It is not clear to me that there are precise figures, but it seems to me fairly clear that the majority of Muslims in some areas lined up with the Ustasha and with the axis powers, and in other areas they lined up with the partisans. Few of them were aligned, if any -- I am sure there probably were a few, but no significant numbers of Muslims were aligned with the Chetniks, with the Serbian Royalist movement. Indeed, it may be worth pointing out that the single large -- the population group which had the single largest loss in the Second World War were the Muslims, the Slav Muslims, in Bosnia and in the Sandzak area, losing something around 80 per cent of the prewar population by the end of the war on the basis of the best figures which can be derived now -- many of them in massacres carried out by the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would like to know to what extent does the difference in religion reflect an ethnic dichotomy? Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: : If you are referring to the Slav Muslims in Bosnia and in Serbia, then I would say there is, first, a difference on the basis of religion which extends into a cultural difference. That kind of difference is regarded by sociologists and anthropologists as constituting an ethnic difference, defining a different ethnic group by a process of self-identification and identification by others. It does not constitute a racially distinct group; race being defined by genetic features. The Albanians in Kosovo area and within parts of Macedonia are Muslim or Islamic by faith, share some of those elements with the Slav Muslims of culture. They have a different linguistic base for their ethnic identity, and I am not sure whether or not anybody could say one way or the other whether they had a separate racial characteristic -- I would say probably not, but I would not pretend to the expertise to make a final judgment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, you mentioned earlier in your evidence when speaking of the breakup of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia the 1986 Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences memorandum; do you recall that? What steps, if any, did Serbia take, the Republic of Serbia take, to address the issues that were raised in this memorandum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under the leadership of President, at that time the President of the League of Communists of Serbia, later to be president of the Republic of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic, Serbia began a process by which the two provinces would be reintegrated within Serbia, that is, the autonomy of the two provinces, if I may remind you, Vojvodina in the north and Kosovo in the south, the autonomy of these two provinces would be removed. Serbia has set about carrying out this process, and in March 1989 accomplished the process in the province of Kosovo, partly in response to assertions of sovereignty by the Albanian majority in the area, but using methods of suppression, including the use and presence of interior ministry troops and elements of the Yugoslav People's Army while that process of reintegration took place, although I should also point out in technical terms the reintegration was accomplished through legal means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps if we can have the map of Yugoslavia on the screen again, please? Could you just direct the cursor to where Kosovo is in relation to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you can pull the cursor down to the point where Montenegro, the "O" of Montenegro leads to the border, around there, if you then, before you move it, can imagine a slightly -- something not quite a diamond or square shaped which would move out slightly into Serbia and then down to the border with Macedonia, and now down, that very approximately would be the area covered by the republic -- by the province of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, did the events that occurred in Kosovo have any influence over what happened in other parts of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbian actions in Kosovo politically asserting Serbian sovereignty and with other means suppressing the autonomy of the local leadership in Kosovo sent signals to the leaders in other parts of Yugoslavia that they would need to look to protect themselves. There was the sense that what Serbia could do to the majority Albanian province of Kosovo, it could try to do in other parts of the SFRY, the sense that what Serbia would do to Kosovo could happen to Slovenia or to Croatia or to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this was a very strong force in political developments in the late 1980s; the sense that Serbia would want to do the same kind of thing that it had done within these provinces in the republics themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in the other republics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1989 Serbia was able to continue the process of, effectively, taking control in areas which it had accomplished first in the two provinces of Vojvodina and Kosovo by working to secure a change in the leadership in Montenegro, so that the Montenegrin leadership, effectively, became an ally -- some would say a puppet -- of the Serbian leadership. This was the first manifestation of the kind of thing which was putting fear into the minds of other Yugoslav leaders. In response to this, the other Yugoslav leaders in Slovenia, in Croatia in particular, began to assert their own sovereignty to revert to the question of the constitutional structure of the SFRY, and to say that really the SFRY was a matter of mutual relations between republics, and that Serbia had no right to interfere and to try to take control of events in the other republics. One particular manifestation of this occurred when Serbia tried to organise a big meeting, a big rally, against the Slovene leadership, but the Croatian and Slovenian authorities stopped the Serbian groups that were going to Slovenia from actually reaching Slovenia by stopping them at the Croatian borders. This gave rise to strong ideas and to actions by Slovenia, in particular, to reassert its own sovereignty, making some changes to its constitution and constitutional law to establish more firmly its sovereign status and to a series of arguments between the various Yugoslav republican leaders, particularly between Slovenia and Serbia over the future of the joint federation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after that, followed from that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The two poll positions, one taken by Serbia, the other by Slovenia, were that the future of Yugoslavia, of the SFRY, lay in a variety of reforms, particularly constitutional reform. Serbia advocated a more centralised system, a return to something which there had been in the past. Slovenia said that the status of the republics under the 1974 constitution had to be reformed and had to be formally codified in a new constitution which would establish a confederal set of relationships between the republics. For Serbia, the idea appears to have been a stronger, more centralised communist control; in Slovenia, the idea appears to have been to move toward a West European style system of competitive party politics. These two positions became very difficult to reconcile.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these positions reflected in elections that were held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1990, first Slovenia, then Croatia moved towards holding competitive multi-party elections. The outcome of those elections resulted in a former -- in the former communist President being re-elected as leader of Slovenia with a government composed of a coalition of opposition groups. At the same time the elections in Croatia saw the election of a strongly nationalist party, the Croatian Democratic Union, under the leadership of the man who became president, Tudjman. Tudjman was a former partisan in general -- in Tito's army. He had been imprisoned as a nationalist and then now returned as a political figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Elections were held in Bosnia towards the end of1990. The results of those elections went largely along the lines of the ethnic composition of the republic -- I think we identified earlier in one of the documents you were given -- slightly less than the proportion of population, in each case voted for what was largely identified as an ethnic party. So, around 30 per cent of the vote went to the -- over 30 per cent of the vote went to the party of democratic action identified largely with the Muslim leadership of Alija Izetbegovic. Around 20 per cent, I think -- I am trying to recall these figures; I do not know them accurately -- went to the Serbian Democratic party organised by Radovan Karadzic, and a smaller proportion in the teens went to the Croatian Democratic Union, the branch of the Tudjman party which operated in Bosnia and Herzegovina. A further 13 per cent or so of the votes went to parties who were looking for a Yugoslav perspective. But the outcome of the elections was to see a Bosnia divided at least on a superficial level politically between different ethnic communities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just dealing with the letters by which these respective parties are often referred to, the Muslim party of Democratic Action, is that referred to as the SDA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is referred to as the SDA, Stranka Demostratska Akcija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Serbian Democratic party is the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Srpska Demokratska Strana.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Croatian Democratic Union is the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, that is Hrvatska Demokratska Zajednica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may have mentioned this, but were there elections also in Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Elections were held in the remaining republics. In Macedonia, the election result went again to a mixture of -- produced a government of reformed communists mixed with some more nationalist groupings; in Serbia and Montenegro, the elections resulted in the substantial -- in a substantial victory for Slobodan Mlosevic and his Serbian socialist party and in Montenegro for his protege, Momir Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, what did the results of these elections mean for Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The results of the elections in the various republics was confirmation of the polarisation of the republics within the SFRY. On the one hand, the communist parties, newly renamed communist parties, in Serbia and Montenegro were elected strongly, giving a strong popular base for the positions taken by the Serbian leadership. At the same time, the outcome of the elections in Slovenia and Croatia, at the other extreme, showed a very substantial, local popular support for the policies being advocated nationally and within the federation by the victors in those cases. The results in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Macedonia, I think, reflect to some extent the divisions within those countries and the relative weakness in which the two republics found themselves within the federation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the next stage in the process of disintegration of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the -- at the same time as these elections were taking place in 1990, different ideas about the future of the Federation were being advocated. The Serbians with a proposal put forward by Borisau Jovic, the Serbian leadership's representative to the collective Federal presidency, Yugoslavia's highest Federal body with a collective presidency with a representative from each of the republics and the autonomous provinces; Jovic put forward the idea of what he called a modernised federation. This was the idea of a more strongly centralised Federation in which power would be concentrated in Belgrade, which was the capital of both Serbia and the federation and would be concentrated in the hands of people who still adhered to the communists' socialist vision for the SFRY. The counter proposal to this was put forward by the leaders of Slovenia and Croatia. For Croatia, I mentioned Franjo Tudjman already, and Slovenia was President Milan Kucan. They advocated a new set of relationships between the republics which would reflect the idea of a confederation; the idea that the sovereignty and independence of each of the republics would be formally and clearly recognised, but that there would continue to be a common existence and the series of common areas in which they would act in common. Between these two proposals, a third proposal emerged. This was put forward by the leaders of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Macedonia. In Bosnia's case Alija Izetbegovic, in Macedonia's case, Kiro Gligorov. This idea was somewhat more akin to the Slovene and Croatian proposal, but reflected the essential weakness of the positions in which Bosnia and Macedonia found themselves, and it called for an asymmetric grouping which would be part confederal, part Federal, depending on the degree of relationship each republic would want to have with the other republics, but still retained the idea of a common framework, but it was a framework in which Bosnia and Macedonia would be able to feel more secure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the Serbian reaction to the confederalist proposal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbia regarded the confederalist proposal as a cover for the idea of breaking up the SFRY completely and establishing wholly independent States. Serbia asserted that if there was a movement towards the confederal option, then Serbia and the Serbs would have the right to retain unity, and that all the territories on which every place where a Serb lived should be regarded as being part of Serbia in that case, and that the areas inhabited by Serbs would then be withdrawn in some way from the republics of Croatia and Bosnia should the confederal option develop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until this stage you have been speaking about, the proposals and counter proposals of the various heads and authorities in the republics themselves, such as Serbia, Slovenia, Croatia and so forth, what was the position during this time of the Federal authorities in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two elements in the Federal authorities. The Federal presidency, I mentioned before, comprised representatives from each of the republics and the autonomous provinces was becoming increasingly irrelevant because it was itself a microcosm of the divisions. Within Yugoslavia there was stalemate within that presidency because half favoured one option, half favoured the other or was somewhere in between. The Federal Government under Prime Minister Ante Markovic was arguing to retain a Yugoslav framework, obviously preferred the Federal option but would have been happy with a confederal option, provided that the common Yugoslav economic space was retained. To try to ensure that the federation preferably but certainly a common Yugoslav space could be retained, Markovic in 1990 -- in 1989 and 1990 introduced a very strong radical programme of economic reform in tying the currency of the denar to the German deutschemark and trying very rapidly and quickly to suppress rampant inflation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How successful was the Prime Minister Markovic's programme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At one level the Markovic programme was very successful. Within a space of six months inflation, for example, was reduced from something like 2,600 per cent to about zero. But, really, I think we have to say the programme was not successful, because following that six-month period it was increasingly undermined by each of the republics asserting its own position, apparently, none of republics having any real interest in supporting the Federal Government and sustaining the continuation of the Federation in the way that Markovic would have wanted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the end of the year, 1990, what was the State of the Federation by this stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that by the beginning of the 1990s the Federation was in need of critical renewal; that it was very difficult to see how there would be any possibility of renewing the Federation as it had been; that the only options were to find a new way of keeping a common Yugoslav existence for the various republics; that the differences between the republican leaderships was increasing translating to differences in the social and ethnic fabric of the territories of the SFRY, and that the country was in probably a final and critical state leading towards dissolution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you use the letters "SFRY", that means the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I use the letters "SFRY" to designate the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia as designated under the 1974 constitution. I use it as a technicality to refer to that particular form of Yugoslavia with that structure of sovereign republics prior immediately to the dissolution of the SFRY, or of the joint, common body of the republics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Federation actually cease to function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that the Federation can be said to have ceased to function on or about 15th May 1991, although for a period before that it was clearly heading towards a critical point at which it would cease to function. That was the day on which the Croatian representative to the Federal presidency Stipe Mesic should have been rotated by an automatic procedure to become the President of the presidency, that is, chief of the ruling Council of the Federation. This procedure established under constitutional laws pursuant to the 1974 constitution should have been an automatic procedure. It had been in all the years prior to this, but it was blocked by the Serbian grouping on the Federal presidency. You will recall I said before the presidency had become largely ineffectual because it was divided between those under the Serbian control, that is, Serbia, the two autonomous provinces, and Montenegro on the one side and the other four republics. Because of this division, Serbia was able to block the rotation of Mesic and at that stage, I think it can be said, the Federation ceased to function. It became clear that the Federal elements no longer had the will to sustain the federation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, firstly, was Croatia's response to this blocking of their Prime Minister becoming Prime Minister of the Federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may correct you -----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: President, I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was -- yes, Mesic was the Croatian representative to the Federal presidency. Croatia had already begun discussing the possibility of seeking full independence at some stage if a confederal arrangement could not be established. It had already taken the decision to organise a referendum on the possible independence of Croatia if the confederal proposals were not accepted. That referendum was held four days later, four days after the issue in the Federal presidency with Mesic on 19th May 1991, and resulted in overwhelming support -- a vote of overwhelming support for the idea of Croatia independence. I should also point out that prior to this in December 1990, in Slovenia, a similar referendum had been organised and had been held on the issue of independence in the eventuality of an agreement not emerging on re-establishing arrangements between the republics along confederal lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the final phase of dissolution begin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The final phase of dissolution may be said to have begun in a number of places. Some people might argue with the memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences in the late 1980s. Some would argue with the Serbian assertion of control over Kosovo in 1989, possibly with the elections in 1990, or with the possibility that in Croatia, as the Croatians tried to restructure the former communist elements, Serbs in a number -- in area in Croatia began to rebel during 1990. But I think it could be at the point I already indicated, when the Mesic rotation was blocked, but I think it can absolutely be said to have taken place on 25th June 1991 when Slovenia and Croatia on the basis of the referendums held declared that the Federation no longer functioned and that they would be independent henceforth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened following the declarations of independence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately after the declarations of independence, an armed conflict began on the territories of the SFRY, and the international community initially in the guise of the European Community began to become involved in the Yugoslav problems.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] I would like to ask Dr. Gow as regards this final dissolution process the following question: What was the reaction, what was the international reaction, was there an immediate recognition of these different countries because Slovenia held its referendum in December 1990 and the declaration of independence came in Croatia in 1991? What happened during that period? What was the reaction of the international community? Secondly, from a legal point of view, which countries were recognised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may answer the first question, and then I may be permitted to clarify? The referendum in Slovenia was held in December 1990 and the referendum in Croatia was held in May 1991, but it was on the same day in 1991, June 25, that both Slovenia and Croatia announced that they would henceforth be independent. So, it was from that point, the 25th June 1991, that we look at the question of the international response to the independence of Slovenia and Croatia. The immediate response to those declarations of independence was that nobody in the outside world accepted or recognised the independent international personality of those two republics. That was not to happen until by -- no outside country was to recognise the independence of those two republics until -- at least not to recognise it formally -- until diplomatic relations ban began to be established in January 1992. On the second question, I think it would be fair for me to say that you asked as a legal question, I do not think I am qualified to give a legal answer, but if you would like me to reformulate the question in a way that I can give an answer as a matter of fact or opinion, I would be happy to do so. Sorry, for being so precise. I do not want to seem to be -- to do the wrong thing.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] When were those countries recognised or admitted within the European communities or within the bodies of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, I shall give a slightly more expansive answer than the question you just asked. It seems to me it is what is required. The States were formally recognised by members of the European Community, by the United States and, broadly, by other countries in January 1992. Prior to that, in October 1991, as part of a conference on Yugoslavia organised by the European Community, the Serbian President, Slobodan Milosevic, had agreed in principle to the independence of the republics within borders. This was on 4th October. I should point out that he was later to say -- to retract some of this agreement. On the basis of that 4th October decision to acknowledge the right of the republics to independence within borders, on 6th October the European Council of Foreign Ministers, that is, the Council of Ministers of the European Community, at a meeting decided that the prospects for the development for the future of the Yugoslav territories would be within the perspective of the right to independence of the republics, but that this should be through a procedure organised by the conference at the end of which there would be agreement between all parties on exactly what the relationships would be. They asked Lord Carrington, the Chair of this conference, to draw up a convention, a draft agreement for relationships between the republics and at a later meeting, I think, on 16th or 18th October agreed that if this document were not to be agreed by all the Yugoslav parties by the end of the year, then the EC would continue to deal with those republics co-operating in this process on the basis of their right to independence. It is in that context that you have to understand the decision in January 1992 to begin to establish diplomatic relations with those Yugoslav republics seeking independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Does your Honour have any further questions that you wish to direct To the witness at this stage or shall I continue? (To the witness): Dr. Gow, you have mentioned the commencement of the armed conflict in Yugoslavia. Turning to that armed conflict, under the constitution, what was the position of the armed forces in Yugoslavia at the commencement of the armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a matter of procedure, may I just ask a question to the Judge?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you might ask ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may go back to the previous answer and add one point to it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By all means do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This would be simply to add that you were talking about the, I think, or we were talking about the dissolution of Yugoslavia and the independence of republics and the completion of the breakup, this would just be to point out that that process can finally be said to have come to a conclusion on 27th April 1992 when the last of the republics declared -- Serbia and Montenegro declared a common future, thereby effectively pronouncing the SFRY completely no longer to exist. It is arguable that it did cease to exist before that, but there can be no doubt from that point onwards. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going on to the commencement of armed conflict in Yugoslavia, under the constitution, the Federal constitution, what was the position of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under the 1974 constitution of the SFRY, the Yugoslav People's Army was one of two elements in a binary defence system. The Yugoslav People's Army, commonly known as the JNA, the JNA was designed to be the first element of defence, the element which would block an attack for a period of 48 hours or more while the second element was mobilised. The second element was a structure of territorial defence forces, some kind of levy en masse in which all the people would become armed. The idea of this system was to deter any potential invader of the country from attacking. It was to persuade them that it simply would not be worthwhile. The JNA was organised by a Federal Secretariat for Defence in Belgrade within the Federation, and the territorial defence organisations were organised by Republican Secretariats for Defence. This two-tier system created a large number of people with arms throughout the territories of the SFRY. In political terms, the JNA was charged with a very pronounced political role under the 1974 constitution. First, it was given the task of being guardian of the territorial integrity and constitutional order of the SFRY. Secondly, under the constitutional laws pursuant to the constitution within the governing framework of the SFRY, that is, the league of communists of Yugoslavia, the set of communist parties ruling Yugoslavia, it was given equal status with the autonomous provinces. So, it was given a clear formal role in the political life of the country within the ruling central committee of the league of communists of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This two-tiered system of armed forces that existed in Yugoslavia, is there an historical explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The idea of having a widely armed population, able to retreat into the mountains and to undermine any invader has some historical precedent in the area. It could be said to go back to the thinking of about Chetnik movements within the Royal Serbian army, but most obviously in terms of Tito's Yugoslavia, the thinking was looking back to the wartime experience in which the partisans as a guerilla force had been able to retreat into the mountain to undermine the occupying powers and gradually transform itself into a formal army which would be victorious in the Second World War. So, there was a strong influence of the partisan thinking from the past in the elaboration of this two-tier system of armed forces for the defence of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the 1948 split with the Soviet Union have any impact upon the military thinking of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Having ended the Second World War as allies of the Soviet Union, a newly ruling communist party leading a would be communist country, relationships between the Soviet Union and Yugoslavia were very good. However, after the split, there developed the very strong prospect that the Soviet Union might want to invade Yugoslavia. This was enhanced at various stages through the 1950s and the 60s when the Soviet intervened in Hungary and Czechoslovakia. This reinforced the Yugoslav's sense that they needed to be able to defend themselves, that they could not rely on anybody else for the defence and, therefore, they began to make preparations though this type of organisational structure I identified, and underpinning that through preparations for conducting this type of long, partisan or guerilla warfare. That meant securing a large -- making preparations to conduct a war in retreat in the mountains, particularly in Bosnia. So there would be large weapon supplies already in place, and it also meant the elaboration and creation of a Defence industry within the SFRY, the largest part of which was located in Bosnia and Herzegovina, because that was envisaged as being the most vital territory in which defence would be carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnic balance in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA, we should look at the JNA in three layers. At the lowest level, it was a conscript force and the ethnic composition represented the ethnic structure of the 18 plus year old population throughout the territories of the SFRY. At the highest level, there was a mechanism known as the national key which ensured that all the top positions within the JNA were allocated as far as could possibly be managed on the basis of ethnic proportionality. However, in the middle layer, representing the bulk of the professional or volunteer soldiers in the officer core and non-commissioned officers, the majority were of Serbian origin. Around 60 per cent of the -- 60 per cent or more of the officer core comprised Serbs, and I think it is fair to say this was a reflection of the experience of the partisans, where the Serbs had formed the core through much of the war through 1943 and 1944 where the fighting was in Bosnia and the core of the partisan movement were the Serbs from Croatia and Bosnia, comprising in 1943 something like 75 per cent of the partisans, although by the end of the war the partisans were far more representative. This is important, I think, to understand because it creates a legacy as you move into the JNA in which there is a tendency for the predominant group, for the largest group within the JNA to be Serbs and for the largest group within those Serbs probably to be Serbs from Croatia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What role did the JNA have in the constitution of 1974 that you mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The role with the JNA, the first level was to preserve, to protect, to be guardians of, the constitutional order of the SFRY and the territorial integrity of the federation. As I said before, I think, there was this further political role established under the constitution through the constitutional laws affecting the role of the league of communists of Yugoslavia in which the JNA was given a strong, formal political role in the political decision-making processes of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was the JNA given a political role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA was given this political role because after some problems of nationalist tension in Croatia in 1971, Tito had formed a reliance with the JNA to restore some sense of Federal order, removing the Croatian leadership, moving on to remove national and liberalising leaderships in other republics. Tito saw the JNA -- I think probably quite rightly -- as being the only body in the SFRY with a clear loyalty to the SFRY as a whole. He, therefore, saw the SFRY -- he saw the JNA within the SFRY in some senses as being his successor. Tito was looking to the possibility that when he died, the JNA would be able to carry on the role of pan Yugoslav arbiter between the various republics within the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] I did not quite follow; what was the political role of JNA in the broad framework which you talked about as regards Tito? Did it implement itself? What tangible form did it take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The formal role of the JNA manifest in the governing body of the SFRY under communist rule. That was the central committee of the league of communists of Yugoslavia. In that structure each of the republics had a set number of delegates to the central committee, each of the autonomous provinces had a reduced number of delegates. If I recall correctly, each of the republics would have 20 representatives and the autonomous provinces would have 15. In that -- the formal role of the JNA was to be given equivalent status with the autonomous provinces and, therefore, to have a formal role of 15 representatives at all stages in the work of the central committee. That was the governing body of the SFRY in real terms. It was also -- it should also be noted that although it was not formally established, the Defence Minister, that is, the top general, was always present -- was often, if not always, present at meetings of the Federal presidency and would always be there as part of the Federal Government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I notice the time. Would now be a convenient time to adjourn?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Yes. This is a very good opportunity to adjourn. We would like to come back at 2.30. (Luncheon adjournment) (2.00 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] We can recommence the hearing with the testimony of Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases. ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW, recalled.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Counsel for the Prosecution, could I take this opportunity to ask you some information? Do you think that Dr. Gow will have completed his testimony by 5.30 or before? What do you think is going to happen there? Do you think it is going to be possible to begin hearing the witnesses at some time who will tell us about what has actually happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my best estimate is that Dr. Gow's evidence will be completed this afternoon, and that there is a very good possibility that we will start with the evidence of the first victim or witness, or eyewitness, I should say.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Thank you. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, prior to the luncheon adjournment, you were speaking of the role of the JNA in former Yugoslavia, and you also mentioned in your evidence a reference to the processes of disintegration o Yugoslavia. Did these forces of disintegration have any impact upon the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The forces working towards the disintegration of Yugoslavia had an impact on the JNA, quite clearly, in terms of the way in which the army was composed. In the final years of the SFRY, problems began to emerge in securing the service of conscripts, many from some parts of Yugoslavia and very notably from Slovenia, were not following orders to turn up to do their military service in the JNA. Political pressures, of course, were being brought to bear on the JNA. I would advance the opinion that the JNA was finding itself in an increasingly difficult position facing pressures from all sides as to how it would position itself, given its constitutional role to safeguard constitutional order, but at the same time with this very strong element from the Serbian community within the officer corps shaping opinions, making it very difficult for people to understand exactly where they were within the JNA. In this situation, it became very difficult both, I suspect, for people within the JNA and for outsiders sometimes to know quite where the JNA stood. One example might be in the course of 1990 and 1991, when local Serbs in Croatia faced with something that they regarded as a fear from the Croatian authorities looked to the JNA, and the JNA at various stages deployed on what it described as a peacekeeping role, trying to stabilize the situation, but a role which increasingly came to appear as giving assistance to the local Serbs in that area. I suspect that some of the people in the JNA probably were giving assistance, and some of the other people in the JNA were simply wanting to retain and maintain as much order within the SFRY as possible. If I might stress at this point, that in looking at this question, from my own point of view, just to underline that much of what I am saying is directed towards what I understand the court, the Tribunal, is interested in today, which is the Serbian project, the war project, which was eventually carried out by people -- by the JNA and by Serbs pursuing an idea. But at the same time it was a complex situation, and I just indicated in Croatia there was a different situation in which the Croatian authorities may in some cases be said to have been culpable for what was happening. So, just to be clear that although it may seem confusing that, on the one hand, a lot of what I have been saying appears one way, I am now saying: "Here were the JNA doing something to help Serbs who may have had a real question".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any changes to the organisational structure of the JNA as a result of these forces of disintegration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think we can clearly say there were changes in the organisational structure of the JNA as a result of these forces of disintegration. There were changes in the structure of the JNA at the end of 1988 and the beginning of 1989. Those changes involved the formation of military districts, and there was argued at the time to be a good military rationale for this. Whatever the exact motivation for the changes at the time, it certainly became apparent as the disintegration, processes of disintegration continued that the structure put in place with the military districts and increased local authority for local -- increased authority for local commanders meant that in some cases the type of ambiguity I was pointing to just now in the Croatian case could lead possibly some local commanders to begin to give assistance to local Serbian communities without any clear sense that this was necessarily coming at that stage in the way of orders from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What relevance, if any, did these changes that were taking place in the JNA have on the events of 1990 and beyond? A.I think the relevance was that the JNA, given its constitutional position, given its own sense of identification as a pan Yugoslav organisation, but with this, as I said before, very strong Serbian element within it, was under pressure. It was under pressure, on the one hand, to protect the SFRY, but that pressure increasingly seemed to mean preserving what might some people would say was a Serbian version of the SFRY, and increasingly its role appeared to come to be looking back in a sense to the past, to the partisan formation and the corps of Croatian and Bosnian Serbs in that movement, to protecting what it was that the Croatian and Bosnian Serbs through the partisans, through the JNA and the SFRY had created. So, that JNA was being put under a lot of pressure by circumstances to move towards a more Serbian position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to this process of moving towards a more Serbian position after the outbreaks of hostilities in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the declarations of independence in June, armed hostilities broke out and the ethnic composition of the JNA changed radically. By the early part of 1992 an army which had been in the conscript, a largely multi-ethnic, which had had the national key principal operating at the top, and which had had representatives from all the Yugoslav communities somewhere in the officer corps, had become largely Serbian dominated, that is to say, most of the non-Serbs in this period left, either disillusioned and trying to seek seclusion or, in most cases, going to join one of the emergent armed forces of the new States. I think this can be clearly seen in terms of the numbers. Of the 180,000 strong JNA in 1991, in May, could be estimated to have around 42 per cent -- approximately 42 per cent of it in total could be said to be Serbs. By the end -- by the middle of 1992 the maximum figure could be about five per cent non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, were there any links between the JNA and the other military groups that you have mentioned, the paramilitary groups that were emerging at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA, or certainly elements from within the JNA, were involved in some of the organisation and armying of paramilitary groups which were to operate on the territory Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. These groups were of two types: Either paramilitary voluntary groups formed by particular leaders, or elements derived from the territorial defence system that I mentioned this morning in areas where Serbs were in the majority. In each case the JNA was involved in the distribution of weapons and the organisation of these forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of these paramilitary groups to which you are referring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The paramilitary groups which were formed by or were associated with particular figures were formed in Serbia and Montenegro. Examples include the "Tigers" organised by Zeljko Raznjatovic (Arkan) -- Arkan being his familiar nom de guerre -- the "White Eagles" organised by Mirko Jovic, the Chetniks organised by Vojislavseselj. There were a number of other smaller groups; each would provide a particular role in situations providing troops of a kind who would not be available to do things that ordinary conscripts -- who would be available to do things that ordinary conscripts would not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was primarily responsible, in your opinion, for setting up and arming these Serbian paramilitary groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbian paramilitary groups just mentioned, both those identified with particular people I just mentioned and the those based around the old territorial defence structure, were set up and armed either by the JNA or by elements of the Federal State Security Service. The key figure -- or the Serbian State Security Service -- the key figures, I believe to be, in the case of the Federal, at the Federal level, the SFRY, the Deputy Interior Minister and Head of the State Security Service at that time, Mihail Kertes, and the head of the Serbian State Security Service, Radmilo Bogdanovic. There were also elements within the JNA involved in this process. If I may give one example? There were reports attributed to tapes -- obtained, tapes made by the last Prime Minister of the SFRY and Markovic which seemed to reveal a conversation between President Milosevic of Serbia and Dr. Karadzic, leader of the Bosnian Serbs in which President Milosevic was instructing Dr. Karadzic to turn to General Uzelac commander of the Banja Luka corps to sort out problems of -- to sort out the issue of weapons provision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You briefly touched on the fact that the paramilitary groups were specifically recruited to do things which the regular JNA army would not do. What role did the paramilitary groups play in the ensuing conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first role that they played was provision of additional manpower. I think we can say that in this situation of transition the JNA was facing manpower problems. I already mentioned that most of the non-Serbs were not going to serve in this Yugoslav army anymore. A number of Serbs were not willing to serve in an army which they perceived now to be taking sides in a war but no longer representing a Yugoslav perspective. So the JNA lacked manpower. So the first role that the paramilitaries played was by making additional manpower available. They were able to make this -- they were able to recruit manpower in this way because they represented a Serbian ideal, I believe. They projected an image of Serbdom which meant that people who were reluctant to fight for a Yugoslav army were prepared to fight for a group identified as being part of a Serbian identity. Of course, there were other reasons for people to fight. In many cases it is because they would be well rewarded for fighting. The second role that they played, in a sense, was as the shock troops. As Serbia and the JNA moved towards a new project and a project which would require certain things to be done, these were troops who were prepared -- I use the term "troops" to describe them; I am not sure if it is wholly appropriate -- but these were troops who were used to go into particular areas to carry out acts sometimes of extreme violence in order to take control of a particular area and to drive out elements of the local population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In doing this was there co-ordination between the JNA and the paramilitary groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There appears to have been considerable co-ordination between the JNA and the paramilitary groups. As the war moved into Bosnia, there seems to have been concerted action with the paramilitary groups playing one role, going into towns, and the JNA playing another role, providing -- encircling towns and providing logistical and artillery support. The planning suggests and the distribution of the JNA forces suggests that they were already prepared to assist paramilitary forces in securing control of particular areas when the war came to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the new political project, I think, a moment ago in your evidence. What did Serbia hope to secure, in your opinion, from the disintegration of Yugoslavia? What was its goals and objectives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a matter of opinion, I would say, I would estimate, that Serbia originally, or the Serbian President, Slobodan Milosevic, originally hoped to have control of all the territories of the SFRY. I would say with some degree of certainty that after the declarations of independence by Slovenia and Croatia, in June 1991, that situation changed, that there was a project established between the Serbian leadership and, at least from August 1991, shared by the JNA leadership, which was to establish the borders of a new entity, that is, a State or a set of territories which would only have Serbian populations and which would be contiguous. This would be what General Kadijevic has described as a common State for the Serb people. It would carved out of parts what was at that stage (and is now) Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the events that then followed in Croatia, particularly after August 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, after the declarations of independence on 25 June 1991, an armed conflict began in Slovenia and in Croatia. In Slovenia it was short lived and featured predominantly forces from the JNA. At the same time a series of armed clashes were occurring in Croatia. These armed clashes became something which I think can be called a major armed conflict from August 1991 onwards when the JNA began in conjunction with Serbia paramilitary groups of various types to pursue this project for establishing the new State. We can take it that this project was decided on probably at that stage from the actions of the JNA, although Kadijevic in the text I mentioned earlier only attributes this decision to some time in the autumn. Clearly, by August the JNA is beginning to pursue the axes of attack which are consistent with the project. That the project did exist and was planned, I think, is confirmed also by the words of General Zivota Panic who was later to become Chief of Staff of the successor Yugoslav army VJ and General Kadijevic himself, both of whom indicates that in Croatia the JNA had to stop sort of its ambitions because of particular pressures at the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did Bosnia fit into this new project?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina was essential to the project I mentioned. The project was to create a set of territories which would be connected to Serbia and which would be for the Serbs and which would be entirely or largely inhabited only by the Serbs. General Kadijevic again makes reference to the keystone position of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serbs for this common State. It was essential in doing this to make sure that key items of infrastructure were secured, including parts of the old, military industrial capability, for the new entity and in doing this to make sure also that all or most of the non-Serbs would be removed from the territories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any political steps taken to support this plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were clear and early signs of the development of this plan in September 1991 in Bosnia and Herzegovina, when the local Serbian leadership of the Serbian democratic party, that is, under Dr. Radovan Karadzic, declared a series of autonomous regions in Bosnia and Herzegovina. At that stage the JNA was conducting a series of exercises and movements across the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina in which elements of the territorial defence force and of the reserve element of the JNA were being mobilised into units so that they would be active and on patrol within those areas. At the same time it seems that something called Crisis Headquarters, that is, shadow secret governments were being prepared by the State Security Services and being put in place to underpin these autonomous regions which would be the framework for the eventual structure -- the framework for the structure of territories that the Serbs would occupy in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any link between the JNA and the Bosnian-Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were clearly some links between the JNA and the Bosnian Serb leadership or between elements in the JNA at least. I think on one example I already indicated was that President Milosevic of Serbia was telling the Bosnian Serb leader, Radovan Karadzic, to make contact with military commanders in order to make preparations for whatever it was that was to come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to the Serbian plan that you mentioned, was there a military aspect to the implementation of this plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military aspect involved the, as I think I again I just mentioned, involved the mobilisation of troops either into the reserve element of the JNA or through territorial defence structures. It also meant the provision of arms through the State Security Service networks into both the territorial defence and other paramilitary groups within the area, and it also meant preparation in the sense of trying to disestablish the territorial defence forces in other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina where Serbs were not in leading positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the response of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina to this activity by the Bosnian Serbs and by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as back as 1990, the President of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, had told Muslims in Bihac that if pressure was put on Bosnia by the Serbs and for disintegration he would look to assert Bosnia's sovereignty and to the prospect and possibility of independence, but what happened when faced -- but this did not emerge. It only emerged in October 1991 when Bosnia and Herzegovina, faced with the declaration of autonomous provinces by the Serbian leaderships in these areas, faced by the activity of the JNA, felt it necessary to assert Bosnia's constitutional sovereignty through a declaration in the parliament. At the same time in the parliament, in September, questions were being asked about the role -- about the activities of the JNA in Bosnia about which there were suspicions at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Bosnian government make application for diplomatic recognition and, if so, when did that occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the events within the territories of the SFRY and internationally developed in the autumn of 1991, Bosnia and Herzegovina following the 16th and 17th December 1991 meeting of the European Council of Foreign Affairs, Ministers of the European Community, made an application to the EC -- to the EC Council for recognition of independent international personality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a Bosnian Serb reaction to this course of events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The application made by Bosnia and Herzegovina in December met with a Serbian response in Bosnia on 9th January. The Bosnian Serb informal assembly announced that if Bosnia were no longer to form part of the SFRY, then the Bosnian Serbs would declare independence. They then went on on 28th February to put in place a constitution and a constitution for the prospective independent territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I think you mentioned earlier, particularly in answer to a question from His Honour, you touched on this area, what did the European Community do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The European Community which had been carrying out the conference on Yugoslavia in the autumn of 1991 and, as a result of the seeming failure of that conference to achieve an overall settlement in December, had decided to open the possibility of those Yugoslav republics seeking recognition of independence to make applications. In doing this, they asked the Advisory Commission of the conference headed by a French constitutional lawyer, I believe, Robert Badinter, to draw up a set of guidelines and then to advise on whether or not it would be -- the guidelines were being met. In the case of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Monsieur Badinter advised the Council that the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina was not -- that the will of the people was not clear, and that it might be advisable to arrange for a referendum to be held in Bosnia and Herzegovina so that the position could be clarified, and the European Council acted on that advice and suggested that the Bosnian authorities conduct a referendum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this advice taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The advice was taken and the Bosnian authorities organised a referendum which was carried out on 29th February and 1st March 1992. The outcome of that referendum was that an overwhelming majority of those who had voted voted for independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but that that represented only 63 per cent of the population as a whole. That was because large numbers of Serbs boycotted the referendum or were prevented from taking part in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, by "Serbs" you mean Bosnian Serbs, of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. Forgive me for not being clear, but I mean Bosnian Serbs who were -- it was Bosnian Serbs who were boycotting the elections, the referendum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the Bosnians do following the referendum, that is, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the referendum results were known on 6th March, the President of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, proclaimed that Bosnia was now independent and sought recognition from the countries of the world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 6th April the European Community Council announced that it would recognise Bosnia and Herzegovina, and as of 7th April 1992 the European Community and its Member States, along with the United States and a number of other countries, proceeded to grant recognition of independent international personality to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a response by the Bosnian Serbs to this course of events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serbs, going back to the announcements made in January and the constitution established in February that I mentioned before, proceeded to declare an independent Serbian republic in Bosnia and Herzegovina on 7th April 1992. In the weeks before that, the end of March, they had also begun a series of military activities in clashes with Croatian forces in two areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name they gave to that part of Bosnia that the Bosnian Serbs declared -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the proclamation of 7th April, it was known as the Serbian Republic in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- sorry, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this was changed simply to what is commonly now called the Republic of Srpske in August 1992. I am sorry if -- I make the record correct. If I just said 1991, I meant 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to the previous question you said that a war then followed or military activity then followed. Who were the participants in this military activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The participants in this military activity on the Serbian side were the JNA, elements of the Serbian territorial -- elements of territorial defence forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina under Serbian leadership and control, and paramilitary groups which came over the border from the territory of Serbia and Montenegro to carry out a series of attacks on particular areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think a couple of times in your evidence you have touched on the role that paramilitary groups play, but perhaps you might expand a little on the co-ordination role that was between the JNA and the paramilitary and the interrelationship between the two, if you would?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA appears to have provided an overall organisational framework for the project that was being pursued, playing a commanding control role, giving logistical assistance and surrounding particular communities, particular towns, with items of heavy artillery. In this, they were acting in conjunction with some of the local Serbian forces. Some of the local Serbian forces but primarily, I believe, paramilitary groups coming from outside Bosnia and Herzegovina, then became involved in actions where towns -- where the forces went into towns and carried out activities in connection with what is commonly known now as ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an official response from Belgrade to these events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this stage we are talking about -- this is in the period April and May 1992 -- the authorities in Belgrade, that is, by that I mean particularly the Serbian leadership, was giving political backing through the forces carrying out this project, and was clearly allowing paramilitary groups, if not organising, paramilitary groups to cross the border. They were also, quite clearly, giving support in terms of the JNA infrastructure that was being used to support their project. However, as the conflict developed and the international perspective on the war appeared to be apportioning blame primarily to Belgrade's forces, the reaction of Belgrade was to try to distance itself from the conflict in Bosnia and to assert that it was no longer involved. The context for this was the prospect that the United Nations Security Council might impose a regime of sanctions on Serbia and Montenegro for its role in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Serbia was trying to maintain the idea that, although politically it could be said to back the cause of Serbs and Croatia and Bosnia, it was not practically involved. The evidence appears to me that in this period it continued explicitly to be involved, and one manifestation of this was the Security Council Resolution 752 of 15th May 1992 in which the Security Council demanded that Belgrade withdraw the JNA forces from Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the same time it also demanded that Croatia withdraw its forces from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you are saying is that the Security Council made it clear that the forces of one State, namely, the Republic of Serbia should not be involved in and should withdraw from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is one of the things that I am saying, yes. If I may, a point of clarification, that the military forces of Belgrade, that is, Serbia and Montenegro, not just the Republic of Serbia, should withdraw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the JNA and Belgrade respond to this pressure that was being applied by the international community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this period, the JNA began transferring all Serbs from Bosnia within the JNA into units operating in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was in preparation for the eventual division of the JNA in which part of the JNA was left behind in Bosnia but renamed the Army of the Serbian Republic -- hereafter I will refer to it as the VRS -- and the other half became known as the Army of Yugoslavia, that is, the force, the military forces in Serbia and Montenegro directly organised and commanded by Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had the JNA prepared itself in advance for this possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seems to me that the transfer of Bosnian Serbs between units within the JNA so that the majority of those serving in Bosnia, something, I believe, around 80 per cent at the time of division in late May 1992 would be Bosnian Serbs, so that it could be then be said that these were Serbs from Bosnia and that they were fighting on their own territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there continued support from Belgrade for the Serbian forces in Bosnia after May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Belgrade military and political leadership, whilst trying to distance itself from the activities of the VRS, seems clearly to have continued to give support; the support coming in a variety of ways, assistance with military medical assistance, for example, wounded Serbian soldiers being taken to the Belgrade military hospital. There also is evidence of both munitions and other supplies going across the border from Serbia into the Serbian held territories in Bosnia, and in some cases evidence of involvement of units from the VJ, that is, the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the command of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The command of the VRS appears to be under -- the command of the VRS is exercised by General Ratko Mladic. General Mladic was a member of the JNA. He was the last JNA commander in Bosnia before the division. His position was then transferred from being commander of the JNA in Bosnia to being commander of the VRS. General Mladic has maintained contacts with the staff, military staff, in Belgrade where he is judged to have a close relationship with the chief of staff of the VJ, General Perisic. There is also some evidence that he has continued to have contact with the Serbian political leadership of Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you, in your opinion, cite this relationship of General Mladic as also being an illustration of the links between Belgrade and the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
